title: Beyond federalism, ConCom's notable reforms
primary_topics: Eight notable non-federalism reforms in the ConCom draft constitution
National territory and South China Sea sovereignty language
Social, economic, and ecological rights expansion
sub_topics: ConCom's Article I national territory -- explicit SCS sovereignty and sovereign rights
Philippine Rise and extended continental shelf
Implicit Sabah claim via 'historic right or legal title'
Article II -- AFP as protector of sovereignty (not people)
Article III -- Bill of Rights demandable vs nonstate actors; international standards
Social and Economic Rights; Environmental and Ecological Rights

stances.claim: Despite its controversial federalism proposals, the ConCom deserves credit for eight notable non-federalism reforms worth serious discussion and eventual adoption.

Article I's clearer national territory language unmistakably upholds PH sovereignty over SCS islands and features, sovereign rights over maritime areas, and 'historic right or legal title' over other territories -- implicitly including Sabah.

Replacing 'the AFP is the protector of the people and the State' with 'the government is the protector of the people' removes the provision being 'misused by political adventurers to justify a military coup.'

Expanding the Bill of Rights to nonstate actors and international standards is significant because multinational companies, international organizations, and powerful individuals already violate fundamental rights of the poor.
stances.rhetorical_move: rights-expansion justification grounded in modern power realities

stances.claim: For the first time in PH constitutional history, defining 'political dynasty' and making the prohibition self-executing is a meaningful anti-dynasty reform.
A double jeopardy exception for due-process deprivation, mistrial, or GAD corrects injustices from precipitate acquittals.
Allowing Congress to change foreign-ownership percentages according to evolving national interest propels the economy while retaining nationalistic protections.

notable_anecdotes: The ConCom's SCS sovereignty language explicitly upholding the arbitral victory while also implicitly alluding to the Sabah claim via 'historic right or legal title' -- without naming Sabah.
The AFP provision analysis: replacing 'protector of the people and the State' with 'the government is the protector of the people' to prevent coup-justification misuse.
The anti-dynasty provision as a 'first' in Philippine constitutional history -- both defining dynasty and making the prohibition self-executing, two elements always absent before.

decision_framework_signals: Separate debate about the whole (federalism) from the merit of individual provisions (eight notable reforms)
Anchor national territory language to all three bases: archipelagic baselines, UNCLOS/international law, and historic right or legal title
Remove constitutional text that can be weaponized for illegitimate purposes (AFP coup justification)
Expand fundamental rights' reach to nonstate actors who now wield power comparable to states
Define prohibited conduct in the constitution itself and make the prohibition self-executing to close the 'as may be defined by law' loophole
Allow legislature to adjust ownership percentages to track evolving national interest rather than locking in fixed percentages
Build double jeopardy exceptions for structural injustice (precipitate acquittals via due-process deprivation or GAD)
one_paragraph_summary: Setting aside the ConCom's controversial federalism proposals, Panganiban credits the consultative committee with eight notable non-federalism reforms worth serious adoption. First, Article I's national territory language unmistakably upholds PH sovereignty over SCS islands and features per the arbitral award, sovereign rights over maritime areas beyond the territorial sea and the extended continental shelf including the Philippine Rise, and -- without naming Sabah -- sovereignty over 'other territories belonging to the Philippines by historic right or legal title.' Second, Article II replaces the AFP provision ('protector of the people and the State') with 'the government is the protector of the people,' removing the text being misused by political adventurers to justify military coups. Third, Article III's Bill of Rights becomes demandable against nonstate actors as well as the state, consistent with international standards -- acknowledging that multinationals, international organizations, and powerful individuals already violate fundamental rights of the poor and weak. Fourth, Social and Economic Rights and Environmental and Ecological Rights are expressly enumerated. Fifth, a double jeopardy exception is provided where the offended party is deprived of due process, there is a mistrial, or the trial court acted with grave abuse of discretion. Sixth, for the first time in Philippine constitutional history, 'political dynasty' is constitutionally defined with self-executing prohibitions -- closing the 'as may be defined by law' gap. Seventh, nationalistic ownership percentages are retained but Congress is empowered to adjust them according to the evolving national interest. Eighth, amendment and revision procedures are simplified with clear separate-voting requirements. The column notes there are more reforms and promises to take them up another time.
